newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Agency accuses Zaire rebels of "Final Solution".
newsitem.headline: Agency accuses Zaire rebels of "Final Solution".

text.p: An aid agency accused Zaire rebels on Friday of aiming for a "Final Solution" in the deaths of 80,000 unwanted Rwandan Hutu refugees.

"Eighty thousand people are condemned to a slow and cruel death. The expression "Final Solution" is not exaggerated," World Food Programme spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said, alluding to Nazi Germany's notorious attempt to exterminate the Jews.
"They (the rebels) want these people to die. There's food over there but these people are starving. If the refugees go into the jungle, they will die. We are powerless."
An aerial search by the United Nations confirmed on Friday that the refugees had fled from camps in eastern Zaire sealed off from relief efforts by Laurent Kabila's rebel troops.

Aid agency concern mounted to outrage and, as a further twist in the tale, the international charity Doctors without Borders warned that the rebels might be using relief organisations to lure the Hutus to their deaths.

"MsF senses that the humanitarian organisations' relief action is being used by the forces of the Alliance to track down groups of refugees who later come under attack," a statement issued in Paris by MsF, one of the aid groups rebels have barred from the area.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, wrote to Kabila urging an immediate search for the missing refugees.
Ogata is "appalled and angry", said her spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole.
"We had up to 100,000 people identified in that area, and now we can find a trace of only couple of thousand," she said.

Kabila's rebels, who have captured half of Zaire and appear poised to end the 31-year rule of Zaire's cancer-stricken President Mobutu Sese Seko, are accused of slaughtering Rwandan refugees in a camp south of the eastern city of Kisangani.

Diplomats said U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy for Africa's Great Lakes region, Richard Bogosian, had been expected to contact Kabila this week to seek support for UNHCR's stalled repatriation programme.
Aid officials say in private the rebels delayed the plan under pressure from Rwanda's Tutsi rulers, swamped by the return of more than half a million Hutu returnees late last year.

The Rwandans are the rump of two million Hutus who fled in 1994 in fear of reprisal for the Hutu-led genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates. They are widely regarded as killers by many Tutsi survivors in their overcrowded homeland.
Ogata is expected to ask governments to increase the pressure on the rebels to help aid agencies when she briefs the U.N. Security Council in a closed-door meeting on Monday.
Apart from Rwanda and Uganda, which back the rebels, diplomats say the governments of the United States and Britain have varying degrees of influence on Kabila.
Many among the refugees are sick and malnourished. They were dying at a rate of 60 a day before they fled their camps.

The World Health Organisation on Friday reported 67 deaths out of 550 cholera cases as of April 19 in Kasese camp which 55,000 refugees fled. In nearby Biaro camp, empty of its 30,000 refugees, it reported two deaths out of three cholera chases.
